usabilityTesting.title: Usability Testing
usabilityTesting.intro: During my User Experience Research internship at ttb, I helped validate digital banking experiences before they reached development — planning research, recruiting participants, running sessions, and presenting findings to cross-functional stakeholders.

scope.label: Scope
scope.value: 12 usability testing projects across multiple financial product verticals

whyWeTested.title: Why We Tested
whyWeTested.body: Before features moved into development, I tested prototypes to identify usability risks, validate user understanding, and surface issues early.
whyWeTested.transition: Each study had different business goals and target users, but the core research question stayed the same:
whyWeTested.quote: Can users understand the experience and complete the task without unnecessary confusion?

academicResearch.title: Automated Detection and Segmentation of Choroidal Neovascularization in OCT Using Deep Learning
academicResearch.short: A comparative deep-learning study exploring automated detection and localization of Choroidal Neovascularization (CNV) in retinal OCT images.
academicResearch.metaNote: Role and research period reflect my personal project record — every research finding on this page is drawn directly from the published paper.

glance.title: Research at a Glance
glance.subtitle: A quick scan of the scope and headline results.

problem.title: The Problem
problem.body1: Choroidal Neovascularization (CNV) is the abnormal growth of blood vessels beneath the retina and is commonly associated with age-related macular degeneration (AMD). CNV can lead to vision impairment.
problem.body2: Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) captures detailed cross-sectional images of the retina and is widely used to detect CNV. But reading those scans is hard: CNV lesions vary in size, shape, and appearance, and OCT images often contain noise, motion artifacts, and other retinal abnormalities that can be mistaken for CNV.
problem.challengesTitle: Why CNV is hard to read
challenges: Easily confused with other retinal abnormalities
problem.closing: Manual interpretation can be challenging and time-consuming — creating an opportunity to explore automated deep-learning approaches for CNV detection and localization.
problem.imageCaption: Healthy OCT (top) vs. OCT with CNV, highlighted (bottom).

objective.title: Research Objective

tasks.title: CNV Image Detection
tasks.body: Determine whether an OCT image contains CNV.

tasks.title: CNV Localization / Segmentation
tasks.body: Identify the CNV region at pixel level.

objective.goal: Identify the optimal architecture for CNV image detection and localization using a balanced OCT dataset.

contribution.title: My Contribution
contribution.intro: As a co-author of the published study, my contribution focused on ground-truth annotation, researching deep-learning approaches, and analyzing candidate architectures to support model selection. The implementation, training, and results presented below reflect the work of the research team as a whole.

items.title: Ground Truth Annotation
items.body: Highlighted CNV regions in OCT images to contribute to the ground-truth annotations used in the study.

items.title: Model Research
items.body: Researched deep-learning architectures and studied their underlying principles, strengths, and suitability for CNV detection and segmentation.

items.title: Model Analysis & Selection
items.body: Compared candidate architectures and contributed to selecting models for experimentation, which were then implemented and trained by other team members.

pipeline.title: Research Pipeline
pipeline.subtitle: From raw OCT scan to model comparison.

dataset.title: Dataset
items: Retinal OCT images, resized to 512 × 512
Evaluation set: 500 manually selected OCT images
250 CNV-positive · 250 CNV-negative (normal)

training.title: Training Setup
items: Models trained with an 80/20 train–evaluation split
Data augmentation: rotation, shifting, zooming, flipping
Google Colab · NVIDIA T4 GPU

models.title: Models Explored
models.intro: Six deep-learning architectures were evaluated under the same experimental setting to compare their performance in CNV detection and localization.

items.name: U-Net
items.description: Encoder-decoder baseline widely used in medical image segmentation.

items.name: Attention U-Net
items.description: Extends U-Net with attention mechanisms to emphasize relevant regions.

items.name: DeepLabV3+
items.description: Uses multi-scale contextual information for semantic segmentation.

items.name: DeepLabV3++
items.description: Refined DeepLab variant that ultimately delivered the strongest overall balance of detection, localization, and training efficiency.

items.name: Mask R-CNN
items.description: Instance-segmentation approach capable of identifying isolated regions.

items.name: Mask R-CNN+
items.description: Modified Mask R-CNN variant evaluated in the study.

classification.title: Classification
classification.blurb: Did the model correctly flag CNV-positive vs. CNV-negative images?

metrics.label: AUC
metrics.description: How well the model separates the two classes.

metrics.label: False Positive Rate
metrics.description: Normal scans wrongly flagged as CNV.

segmentation.title: Segmentation
segmentation.blurb: Once flagged, how precisely did the model outline the CNV region?

metrics.label: Precision
metrics.description: Of the pixels marked CNV, how many really were.

metrics.label: Recall
metrics.description: Of the true CNV pixels, how many were found.

metrics.label: IoU
metrics.description: Overlap between predicted and true CNV region.

results.title: Results — Classification
results.intro: All six models were evaluated on the same 500-image balanced set. DeepLabV3+ and DeepLabV3++ came out on top.
results.highlight: DeepLabV3+ and DeepLabV3++ achieved the highest classification accuracy and AUC — both at 99.4%, with a 0% false negative rate and a low 1.2% false positive rate.

segmentationResults.title: Segmentation Comparison
segmentationResults.intro: Detecting CNV is only half the task — the model also has to outline it accurately. This is where the models pulled apart the most.
segmentationResults.tableCaption: Segmentation performance across all six models (%)
segmentationResults.imageCaption: Original · Ground Truth · six model outputs, one representative case.
segmentationResults.finding: DeepLabV3++ achieved the strongest overall localization performance — the highest F1-score and IoU among all six models, with recall competitive with the best-performing alternatives.

whyDeepLab.title: Why DeepLabV3++?
whyDeepLab.intro: Considering both performance and training efficiency, DeepLabV3++ emerged as the strongest overall candidate in this study.
reasons: Strong classification performance, tied for the best in the study
Highest overall segmentation F1-score and IoU
High recall — competitive with the best models at finding true CNV regions
whyDeepLab.trainingTimeCaption: Training time by model (minutes) — lower is faster
whyDeepLab.trainingNote: DeepLabV3++ required substantially less training time than U-Net while achieving stronger overall classification and segmentation performance.

limitations.title: Where the Models Struggled
limitations.intro: Strong headline metrics don't tell the whole story. Looking closely at individual cases surfaced real, recurring failure patterns across every model — not just DeepLabV3++.
items: Under-segmentation of low-contrast CNV regions
Difficulty delineating precise lesion boundaries
False positives on structures that resemble CNV, like the RPE layer
Conflicting segmentations between models on the same image — a sign of instability
Sensitivity to image format (grayscale vs. RGB), especially for models pretrained on natural images
Small or low-contrast CNV regions were sometimes missed

future.title: Future Research Directions
items: Ensemble / model-fusion approaches for more stable predictions
Conditional Random Fields (CRFs) to sharpen mask boundaries
Morphological operations and shape priors
Transformer or hybrid CNN-transformer architectures
Explainability tools — Grad-CAM and SHAP — to build clinical trust
Expanded datasets to improve model robustness and reliability.
